source_text: Εἶδον ἐν τοῖς κάτω μέρεσι, κολάσεως μὲν βάραθρον τοὺς δυσσεβεῖς δεχόμενον, εὐσεβέσι δὲ χῶρον ἕτερον ἀνειμένον. Ἐλογισάμην δὲ πάντα ὅμοια ὑπάρχειν παρὰ Θεῷ νομίζεσθαι καὶ κρίνεσθαι, ταυτὸν εἶναι δικαίους καὶ ἀδίκους, λογικὰ καὶ ἄλογα. Χρόνον τε γὰρ ἅπασιν ὁμοίως ἐπιμεμετρῆσθαι, καὶ θάνατον ἐπηρτῆσθαι, ταυτόν τε εἶναι παρὰ Θεῷ κτηνῶν τε καὶ ἀνθρώπων φῦλα, διαφέρειν δὲ ἀλλήλων, μόνῳ τῷ ἐνάρθρῳ τῆς φωνῆς· συμβαίνειν δὲ αὐτοῖς ἅπαντα παραπλήσια, καὶ τὸν θάνατον χωρεῖν, οὐδὲν μᾶλλον ἐπὶ τὰ λοιπὰ τῶν ζώων, ἤπερ καὶ ἐπ᾽ ἀνθρώπους. Πνεῦμα γὰρ πᾶσιν ὅμοιον εἶναι, καὶ πλέον ὑπάρχειν ἐν ἀνθρώποις μηδέν, ἀλλὰ πάντα ἑνὶ λόγῳ εἶναι μάταια, ἀπὸ τῆς αὐτῆς γῆς λαβόντα τὴν σύστασιν, καὶ εἰς τὴν αὐτὴν γῆν ἕξοντα τὴν ἀνάλυσιν. Ἄδηλον γὰρ εἶναι περί τε τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων ψυχῶν, εἰ ἀναπτήσονται ἄνω, καὶ περὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ἃς τὰ ἄλογα κέκτηνται, εἰ κάτω διαρρυήσονται. Καὶ ὅ μοι ἐδόκει μηδὲν ἕτερον ὑπάρχειν ἀγαθόν, εἰ μὴ τρυφὴ καὶ τῶν παρόντων χρῆσις. Οὐ γὰρ εἶναι πάλιν ᾠήθην, ἐπὶ τὴν ἀπόλαυσιν τούτων ἐλθεῖν δυνατόν, ἅπαξ ἀνθρώπῳ θανάτου γευσαμένῳ.
thought_title: Solomon sees the fate of the impious and pious below, and reflects on the equality of all before God
orientation: Solomon (reported) describes a vision of the underworld where the impious are received into a pit of punishment and the pious into a different, untroubled place, then reasons that God regards all alike — humans and animals share the same breath, death, and origin, and it is unclear whether human souls rise or animal souls descend.
pass_a_gloss: I saw in the lower parts, a pit of punishment receiving the impious, but for the pious another place untroubled. I reckoned that all things are considered alike and judged by God, the righteous and the unrighteous to be the same, the rational and the irrational. For time has been measured out equally to all, and death hangs over them, and the races of beasts and of humans are the same before God, differing only by the articulated voice; and all things happen to them similarly, and death goes to them, nothing more upon the rest of the animals than upon humans. For the spirit is alike to all, and there is nothing more in humans, but all things are vain by one account, having taken their composition from the same earth, and they will have their dissolution into the same earth. For it is unclear concerning human souls, whether they will breathe upward, and concerning the rest which the irrational possess, whether they will flow downward. And what seemed to me to be no other good, except enjoyment and use of the present things. For I did not think it to be possible again to come upon the enjoyment of these, once a human has tasted death.

choices.why: Glossary does not cover this compound; literal rendering matches the visionary imagery of a pit receiving the impious.
Contrasts with the pit of punishment; 'untroubled' captures the sense of a place of ease for the pious.
Death is portrayed as fitted to all alike; 'fitted' preserves the passive sense of being equipped or appointed.
Only difference noted between humans and beasts; 'articulated' conveys jointed, distinct speech.
Literal directional sense of ἀνα- + πνέω; matches the uncertainty about human souls rising.
Διαρρέω implies flowing through or down; retains the fluid image contrasted with breathing upward.

bible_refs.note: For the fate of humans and beasts is the same; one breath for all; all from dust and return to dust; who knows if the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of beast goes downward?
Nothing better than enjoyment of present good; this is from the hand of God.

pass_b_english: I saw in the lower regions a pit of punishment that receives the impious, while the pious have another place, untroubled. I considered that all things are reckoned alike by God and judged alike; the righteous and the wicked are the same, the rational and the irrational are the same. For the same span of time has been measured out for all, and death hangs over them; the kinds of beasts and of humans are the same in God’s sight, differing from each other only by the articulated voice. They experience everything in much the same way, and death comes no more upon the other animals than upon humans. For all have a similar spirit, and humans have no advantage over them, but all things are empty in a single word, having taken their composition from the same earth and having their dissolution into the same earth. For it is unclear concerning human souls whether they will fly upward, and concerning those of the irrational creatures whether they will flow downward. And it seemed to me that nothing else is good except enjoyment and the use of present things. For I did not think it possible to come again to the enjoyment of these, once a human being has tasted death.

problems.why: ἀναπτήσονται means 'fly up/ascend'. 'Breathe upward' is wrong and loses the image of the soul rising.

problems.quote: death goes to them no more than it goes to the other animals
problems.source_quote: τὸν θάνατον χωρεῖν, οὐδὲν μᾶλλον ἐπὶ τὰ λοιπὰ τῶν ζώων, ἤπερ καὶ ἐπ᾽ ἀνθρώπους
problems.why: The comparison is garbled. The source says death comes no more to the other animals than to humans. The English makes the animals the benchmark and is confusing.
problems.fix: and death comes no more upon the other animals than upon humans

edits.old: death goes to them no more than it goes to the other animals
edits.new: death comes no more upon the other animals than upon humans

fixed: Changed 'breathe upward' to 'fly upward' to match ἀναπτήσονται (fly up/ascend).
Fixed the garbled comparison: source says death comes no more to the other animals than to humans; English had the benchmark reversed and was confusing.

problems.quote: death has been fitted to all alike
problems.why: ἐπηρτῆσθαι means death hangs over or impends, not that it has been fitted.
problems.ruling: ἐπηρτῆσθαι (from ἐπαρτάω) means death hangs over or is suspended above all. 'Fitted to' loses that impending sense and misleads.

edits.old: and death has been fitted to all alike

fixed: 'death has been fitted to all alike' changed to 'and death hangs over them' to reflect ἐπηρτῆσθαι (impends/hangs over) per the source.
